en: 1. The First Precept on Delivering from Peril and Suffering.

The Buddha said: “O Son of the Buddha, after my parinirvāṇa, in this evil age, if you see non-Buddhists, various wicked people, or bandits selling images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or one’s parents, or selling the sūtras and the Vinaya, or trafficking in them—”
If one sells bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs,
or even sells those who have set their minds on awakening— bodhisattvas and practitioners of the Way—
or subjects them to official service or makes them slaves for all people; [this constitutes a grave offense].
When a bodhisattva sees these things,
they should give rise to a mind of compassion and skillfully provide protection and rescue,
teaching and transforming beings everywhere.

To take objects to ransom Buddha or Bodhisattva images, as well as the scriptures and Vinaya of all those who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment—whether monks, nuns, or bodhisattvas—and fail to redeem them, constitutes a minor offense.
To sell scriptures or images for profit carries the fault of causing damage and dishonor.
Those who trade in human beings suffer the distress of being held in secret confinement.
Since the Great Being’s resolve is to protect the Dharma and relieve suffering,
he ought to redeem them according to his ability.
If one does not redeem or rescue [others], one violates respect and violates compassion;
therefore, this was established as a precept.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, bodhisattvas are able to provide protection and rescue for all sentient beings who have fallen into various fears, such as those caused by lions, tigers, wolves, malevolent spirits, kings, bandits, water, or fire.
To cause them to leave such places of fear— whether great or small,
and whether shared or unshared—
is the seventh category of offense for a Śrāvaka who sees his retinue being sold and does not redeem them.
Regarding scriptures, images, and other persons, no specific prohibitions are seen;
a Bodhisattva must never fail to save anyone,
except when it is beyond their power.
The seven classes of followers are fellow students.
Regarding the passage in the text concerning those who sell images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or their parents,
one interpretation states:
This chapter is the great compassionate father and mother;
therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva is like a father and mother.
One interpretation states:
One carves or casts images in the likeness of one's parents,
such as in the case of Ding Lan and others;
therefore, it is called "the image of the parents."
Regarding the section on the selling of bhikṣus, the subsequent passage clarifies the redemption of practitioners.
Within the text, it refers only to "those who follow the Way" (道人) because they cause the most extensive harm and damage.
One should also rescue others who have fallen into calamity; this is the principle. **The Second Precept:

Not Keeping Harmful Creatures.** If a Buddha’s disciple does not engage in the trade of swords, staves, bows, or arrows; nor use light scales or small measures; nor seize the property of others by relying on official authority or influence; nor, with a harmful intent, bind, destroy, or exploit them; nor raise cats, raccoons, pigs, or dogs—if one intentionally raises such creatures, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*). From here below, regarding the eight precepts that encompass [the community] through the Dharma, there are two parts.
The first seven are subsumed under the dharma of practice,
while the eighth is subsumed under the dharma of teaching.
Within the subsumption under practice, there are further two [divisions].
The first two precepts clarify conduct that avoids transgressions;
the latter five precepts clarify conduct that embraces virtue.
Within the conduct that avoids transgressions:
First, one is freed from the fault of causing harm;
later, one is freed from the fault of negligence.
Because keeping [such creatures] involves harming them and thus contradicts the practice of compassionate gathering, it was prohibited and ordered to be abandoned.
Both the great and the small [precepts] are equally regulated; the seven classes of followers collectively maintain them.
Within the text, six matters are fully enumerated.
First, one must not keep swords, staves, bows, or arrows.
This is to prevent the fault of killing and harming.
It was established because it violates the "gathering of wholesome qualities" (kuśalasaṃgrāhaka) within the tenth precept mentioned previously.
Now, within these precepts, this is established because it contravenes the gathering of wholesome qualities;
it is established so as to cause the benefit of sentient beings.
Second, one must not engage in trade using light scales or small measures.
This prevents the fault of theft and damage.
Third, taking another's wealth and goods by means of official authority or power.
This corresponds to the seventeenth rule previously mentioned: "Begging for things by means of one's power."
Now, this precept is established because of a request made on behalf of another;
it likewise serves to prevent theft and damage.
It is bound by four harmful mental states.
This means that although the mind may intend to cause harm or distress, it does not necessarily result in actual injury.
Fifth is "destroying what has been accomplished," which refers to destroying the results achieved by others through their efforts.
Sixth, one should not keep long-tailed cats and the like,
as they may cause harm at a distance; however,
there is no offense if one rescues them when they are in imminent danger.

3. The Third Precept on Not Engaging in Deviant or Idle Conduct. If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind, observes all men and women fighting, or armies, generals, and bandits contending; nor shall they listen to the sounds of conchs, drums, horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, *konghou* lutes, singing, shouting, or the music of performers. They must not engage in *chuyu*, go-boards, *parase* (chess), *tanqi*, *liubo*, ball-bouncing, stone-throwing, *touhu*, *quandao*, *badao*, *xingcheng*, *zhua*, mirrors, milfoil stalks, willow branches, or begging bowls, nor use skulls to practice divination. They must not act as messengers for thieves or bandits; none of these things shall be done. If one intentionally commits such acts, they violate a minor defiling offense (*qinggou-zui*). This precept is established because it contravenes right livelihood.
The regulations for the large and small [robes] are identical;
they are not shared among the seven classes of followers. Within the text, five matters are enumerated.
First, one must not watch various fights;
this is prohibited for both monastics and laypeople alike unless there is a specific necessity.
Second, one must not listen to various musical performances.
If it is for one's own amusement, both monastics and laypeople are prohibited;
if it is for making offerings to the Triple Gem, both monastics and laypeople are permitted;
if it is performed by oneself, it is prohibited for monastics but permitted for laypeople.
Third, one must not engage in various forms of play;
this is prescribed for both monastics and laypeople alike.
Fourth, one must not practice divination or fortune-telling.
For the benefit of both monastics and laypeople, this is prescribed as a joint precept.
It is lawfully indicated that for laypeople, five [prohibitions] are permitted;
however, one must not engage in the commission of banditry or serve as a messenger for such purposes.
The previous eleven precepts regulated public and official missions;
this precept regulates private and clandestine missions.
This, too, is prohibited for both monastics and laypeople alike.

4. The Precept of Not Recollecting Other Vehicles. If a Buddha’s disciple upholds the prohibitive precepts, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they should recite these precepts during the six periods of day and night as if they were a vajra. They should be like one carrying a life-preserving float intending to cross the great ocean, or like the bhikṣu bound by grass. They should constantly give rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna, knowing for themselves: "I am a Buddha who is not yet perfected; the Buddhas are those who have already attained perfection. They should resolve upon bodhicitta, never allowing it to depart from their minds even for a single thought-moment. If they give rise to a single thought of the Two Vehicles or of non-Buddhist paths, they commit a secondary offense (light defilement). The following five precepts clarify the practice of gathering wholesome deeds.
First, it precludes mindfulness of other vehicles' paths;
next, it precludes the failure to give rise to great vows;
and finally, it precludes the failure to make firm pledges.
Next, [the text] refutes the failure to cultivate detachment.
Next, it refutes the failure to show deference between elders and juniors.
First, regarding those who do not keep other vehicles in mind:
Fearing that it might impair the Great Practice, this regulation was established:
monastics and laypeople study together, but those of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not share [the same precepts].
Because the practices followed by each differ,
there are three items listed in the text: first,
the method for protecting and reciting the precepts.
"Those who uphold the prohibitive precepts" refers to those who maintain both the natural (*prakṛti*) and the proscribed (*pratikṣepa*) precepts;
"those who recite these precepts six times during the day and night" refers to this.
Whether regarding the words or the meaning, one recites and maintains them without forgetting;
this is "like a vajra" because the mind is held with such firmness that it cannot be destroyed by any cause or condition.
One who carries a life-preserving float intending to cross the great ocean cherishes and guards it, desiring that it not leak;
this account is derived from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Regarding the "grass-tethered bhikṣu," this refers to one who is cautious,
reverently maintains the precepts, and does not dare to transgress them;
this account is derived from the *Nidāna-sūtra*.
Second, they give rise to Mahāyāna faith,
realizing for themselves that although they possess Buddha-nature, they are yet to become Buddhas.
Because they have not yet cultivated [the causes].
The Buddhas are those who have already attained Buddhahood;
they have already cultivated the sublime causes and realized the supreme fruit.
Third, regarding "generating the bodhicitta so that it does not depart from the mind in every thought-moment":
this refers to directing the mind toward the great fruit.
No other thoughts shall intervene. If even a single thought arises that falls short of this, it constitutes an offense, as will be clarified below. **Chapter Five:

Making Vows and Aspiring for the Precepts** If a Buddha’s disciple constantly makes all vows—vowing to be filial toward parents and respectful toward teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem; vowing to obtain a good teacher, fellow students, and virtuous spiritual friends who constantly instruct them in the Mahayana sutras and vinaya; vowing to understand the Ten Approaches, the Ten Nurturings, the Ten Vajra-like Stages, and the Ten Grounds; and vowing to practice according to the Dharma and firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts, never departing from them in thought after thought even at the cost of their own body and life—if any Bodhisattva does not make these vows, they commit a minor offense (light defilement). A vow is like a skillful driver.
One is about to proceed toward the supreme fruit;
yet if one does not make a vow, there is nothing upon which to rely for practice. Therefore, this is established as a rule to compel the making of a vow.
The seven classes of practitioners study together,
yet those of greater and lesser capacity do not share [the same realization], because that which they seek differs.
Regarding the instruction that one should constantly give rise to all vows within the text:
this means that one should generate vows according to each specific matter so that not a single one passes by in vain,
as explained in the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śīla-viśuddhi-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, because there are ten great vows, it is said that one should "arouse all vows.
As for these ten great vows,
they are as explained in the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*.
Regarding the section on filial piety and obedience below, among all the aspirations raised,
the essentials are briefly set forth as three or five.
First is being filial and obedient toward one's parents, teachers, and the assembly.
Do not violate your supreme vows of gratitude.
Your parents have undergone the toil of giving you life and raising you;
your teachers and the assembly have performed the merit of instructing and guiding you.
Since they have both bestowed supreme kindness, one ought to accord with filial piety toward them.
As for the wish to encounter an excellent teacher, fellow students, and virtuous friends,
this is a prayer for the meeting with superior conditions.
Those who have constantly instructed me in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, and who,
by relying upon and inheriting this sublime teaching,
aspire to the ten stages of departure and up to the ten bhūmis.
The vow for entering the stage of superior understanding:
May I attain realization and practice in accordance with the Dharma;
may I gather the vows of supreme conduct.
Regarding "upholding the Buddha’s precepts" and so forth:
this refers to the vow to protect and maintain the supreme precepts.
Because the precepts serve as the foundation for practice, they are specifically singled out.
6. The Sixth Precept on Making Vows and Self-Commitment: If a disciple of the Buddha, having made these ten great vows, upholds the prohibitions of the Buddha and makes this vow, saying:
I would rather cast this body into a great pit of blazing,
fierce fire or onto a mountain of blades than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time by engaging in impure conduct with any woman.
Furthermore, he makes this vow:
"I would rather have my body encircled on all sides by a thousand layers of glowing iron mesh than ever receive any clothing from a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts."
Furthermore, he makes this vow:

"I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and great torrents of fierce fire with this mouth for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever eat the food of a hundred flavors offered by a faithful donor with a mouth that has broken the precepts."
He further made this vow:
"I would rather let this body lie upon a ground of great currents, fierce fires, iron nets, and glowing red-hot iron;
I shall never, with a body that has broken the precepts, accept the hundreds of kinds of seats offered by faithful donors."
Furthermore, he made this vow:

"I would rather endure three hundred spear thrusts with this body for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever receive the hundred-flavored medicines and medical provisions from a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts."
He further made this vow:
"I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever receive,
with a body of broken precepts, the thousandfold offerings of houses, dwellings, gardens, and fields from faithful donors."
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"I would rather have this body, from head to foot, smashed with an iron hammer until it is like fine dust,
than ever receive the respectful prostrations of a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts."
He further made this vow:
"I would rather have my two eyes gouged out by a hundred thousand heated iron knives and spears than ever look upon the beautiful forms of others with a mind that violates the precepts."
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"I would rather have my sense organ of hearing pierced by a hundred thousand iron awls for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever listen to pleasant sounds with a mind that violates the precepts."
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"I would rather have my nose cut off by a hundred thousand blades than ever,
with a mind of broken precepts, greedily smell various fragrances."
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"I would rather have my tongue cut off by a hundred thousand blades than ever,
with a mind that violates the precepts, consume the pure food of a hundred flavors offered by others."
Furthermore, he made this vow:
"I would rather have my body hacked to pieces with a sharp axe than ever,
with a mind of broken precepts, crave pleasant tactile sensations."
Furthermore, one should make this vow:
"May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood.
If a Bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense (light defilement). To have it in the mind is to form a vow.
One forms a vow with the mouth and body because one fears being swayed by conditions; thus, one establishes a vow to bind oneself.
There is no commonality between the great and the small [vows].
Regarding the "seven classes of fellow students," the text states that they have already made the ten great vows; however,
some versions of the text state that they have made thirteen great vows.
This refers to the thirteen vows established below.
Because he first generated them within his mind and subsequently formulated them verbally, it says "having generated.
If one speaks of the "ten great vows," [it is because]...
There are another ten vows which are first generated by bodhisattvas at the initial stage of mind,
as described in the *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra*.
How does a bodhisattva set out for enlightenment?
By what karmic practices does one accomplish the bodhicitta?
A bodhisattva who has resolved upon enlightenment dwells on the stage of wisdom.
First, one should firmly resolve upon the right vow to gather in and sustain all immeasurable sentient beings.
One seeks unsurpassed enlightenment in order to rescue, protect, and deliver them,
leaving none remaining.
They cause all beings to ultimately attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Therefore, the initial arousal of the mind of awakening has great compassion as its foremost element;
by means of this compassionate heart, one is able to give rise to ten successive and increasingly superior great right vows.
What are the ten? They are:
first, may the roots of goodness planted by me in previous lives as well as in this present body be bestowed upon all infinite sentient beings through these roots of goodness.
May all together be dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi,
so that this vow of mine may increase from moment to moment;
in every life and birth, may it always remain fixed in my mind and never be forgotten.
First, may I be protected by dhāraṇīs.
Second, having dedicated these roots of goodness toward great enlightenment,
may I always be able to make offerings to all Buddhas in every place of birth.
May I never be born in a Buddha-less land.
Third, having been born in the lands of all Buddhas,
may I always be able to draw near to them and attend upon them at their side.
Like a shadow following a form,
may I not be separated from all Buddhas for even a single moment.
Fourth, having attained intimacy with the Buddhas, may I...
May he preach the Dharma to me according to what is appropriate for me,
so that I may achieve the five supernormal powers of a bodhisattva.
Fifth, having achieved the five supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, may I—
Thus, one penetrates the conventional truth as it is circulated through provisional designations;
one understands the ultimate truth and attains the wisdom of the true Dharma according to its suchness.
Sixth, may I, having attained the wisdom of the true Dharma,
with an insatiable mind, explain, instruct, benefit, and gladden sentient beings,
causing them all to attain realization and understanding.
Seventh, may I, having brought all sentient beings to understanding and liberation,
travel by the Buddha’s spiritual power to all worlds throughout the ten directions without exception, making offerings to all Buddhas,
hearing and receiving the true Dharma, and extensively gathering in sentient beings.
Eighth: May I, having received the true Dharma from all Buddhas, be able to accordingly turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
May all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who hear my Dharma or hear my name [attain liberation].
One immediately attains the relinquishing of all afflictions and the arousal of the bodhicitta.

Ninth, one makes the vow: "May I cause all sentient beings to arouse the bodhicitta, and having done so, may I always follow and protect them, removing what is unbeneficial and bestowing immeasurable happiness."
They sacrifice their bodies, lives, and wealth to gather in sentient beings and shoulder the burden of the True Dharma.
Tenth, they vow: "Once I have been able to shoulder the burden of the True Dharma, though I practice the True Dharma, my mind shall have nothing to practice."
Just as all bodhisattvas practice the true Dharma while having nothing to practice,
yet they do not fail to practice in order to transform sentient beings and never abandon their right vows—
this is called the ten great right vows of the bodhisattva who has resolved upon enlightenment.
These ten great vows pervade the realm of sentient beings and encompass all vows as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Only when sentient beings are exhausted will my vows come to an end.
Yet sentient beings are truly inexhaustible,
and this great vow of mine shall likewise never end.
Upholding the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, he made this vow, speaking these words as a solemn oath of self-restraint.
Among the thirteen vows, the first twelve constitute the vows for guarding the precepts,
while the final one constitutes the vow for realizing the fruit.
Within these twelve, the first seven guard the *vinaya* (discipline) precepts.
The latter five constitute the precepts for guarding the five faculties.
Among the seven [precepts], the first six involve making vows regarding specific objects;
since the female object is easily defiled and extremely fearsome, it is treated with particular gravity.
Therefore, he made a partial vow for protection.
The subsequent six pairs of vows established for offerings are essentially the same in their general meaning as those taught in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* regarding noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*).

Chapter Seven: The Dhūta Precept of Seasonal Practice. This precept of seasonal dhūta may also be called the dhūta precept of avoiding calamities. O Sons of the Buddha, one should always practice the dhūta of the two seasons.
He practiced seated meditation during both winter and summer,

observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*). He constantly maintained a willow branch, cleansing powder, the three robes, a water jar, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, a mendicant’s staff, an incense burner, a water filter, a hand towel, a small knife, a fire-starter, tweezers, a rope bed, as well as the Sūtras and Vinaya, and images of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas.
When a bodhisattva practices the dhūta austerities or travels from place to place,
even if they journey for a hundred or a thousand *li*,
these eighteen kinds of items always remain with their person.
Regarding the dhūta practitioner: from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month,
and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month—
during these two periods, these eighteen kinds of items must always accompany the body.
Just as a bird has two wings,
so too, on the days of the *poṣadha*,
a newly initiated bodhisattva should recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts during the fortnightly *poṣadha* ceremony.
If it is said that when observing the precepts one should recite before the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas:
if there is one person performing the *poṣadha*, that one person shall recite;
even if there are two, three, or up to a hundred thousand people, only one person shall recite.
The reciter shall sit on a high seat and the listeners on lower seats;
each shall wear the nine-striped, seven-striped, or five-striped *kāṣāya* robe.
When entering the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one should likewise act in accordance with the Dharma in every detail.
When practicing the dhūta austerities, do not enter dangerous places,
nor regions with wicked rulers,
nor where there is a wicked king.
The terrain is uneven, with dense vegetation and deep ravines;
it is beset by lions, tigers, and wolves,
as well as the perils of water, fire, and wind.
As well as bandits,
venomous snakes on the roads,
and all places of peril.
None of these may be entered.
During the practice of *dhūta* austerities, while traveling on the path, and even during the summer retreat of *varṣā*,
one must not enter any of these difficult places.
If one enters intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light impurity). *Dhūta* is translated here as "shaking off";
it refers to shaking off attachments within the mind.
Because one can adorn the precepts by remaining serene beyond the mundane world,
one should practice accordingly; in such practice, one does not discriminate regarding the location.
One may suffer premature death;
furthermore, those who have not yet abandoned desire find no peace of mind during times of calamity.
Therefore, one must avoid such dangers.
One's practice shall accord with what is appropriate.
This rule is established for all seven assemblies alike.
Śrāvakas avoid such difficulties.
It should likewise be regulated in the same way.
As for the two times when [the practice] is constantly observed, it need not be formally regulated.
Regarding the statement in the text that one should always practice *dhūta* during these two times:
Because the cold and heat during the two seasons of spring and autumn are moderate and do not cause harm,
[the practice] is established for these two times.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Question: Why is it called the merit of *dhuta*?
Answer: It is, for example, like wool or cotton in the world that has not yet been beaten, nor carded, nor teased, nor split;
at that time, they stick together, being neither soft nor light.
It cannot bear being fashioned into thread, cord, felt, or rugs;
yet when it is whipped, patted, teased, or carded,
it then becomes dispersed, soft, supple, and light.
It is capable of being fashioned into thread, yarn, woolen cloth, or rugs.
In the same way, this practitioner, through craving for food and drink, causes the mind to become stained by attachment to various foods and drinks;
through craving for clothing, he causes the mind to become stained by attachment to various garments.
Due to attachment to bedding, the mind becomes stained and attached to various types of bedding;
through such ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*), he is able to purify and cultivate himself, making his mind upright and sincere.
Being supple, light, and subtle, one possesses the capacity for endurance;
by following and relying upon these qualities, one is able to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Therefore, they are called the "merits of ascetic purification" (*dhūtaguṇa*).
Regarding food and drink, there is the craving for fine food and the craving for eating excessively, both of which can obstruct the cultivation of wholesome qualities.
Desiring to eliminate the craving for fine food,
one should always expect to beg for alms and practice begging for alms in successive order.
In order to sever craving for overeating,
one should eat only during a single sitting, first ceasing before beginning again.
Regarding clothing, there are three kinds of craving that can obstruct the cultivation of virtue.
First, craving for many garments;
second, craving for soft touch;
third, craving for superior and exquisite [garments].
In order to sever craving for many garments, one maintains only the three robes;
in order to sever craving for soft textures, one maintains only garments of wool;
in order to sever craving for superior finery, one maintains rag-robes.
Regarding various furnishings, there are four kinds of craving that can obstruct the cultivation of wholesome qualities:
first, craving for social bustle;
second, craving for dwellings.
Third is greed for the pleasure of reclining and the pleasure of lying down;
fourth is greed for bedding and seats.
One dwells in an araṇya in order to sever greed for the clamor and bustle of society.
In order to sever craving for dwellings,
he constantly dwells beneath trees, in the open air,
and among burial mounds. Furthermore, in order to sever craving for sensual pleasure, he constantly dwells among burial mounds.
One constantly maintains a sitting posture in order to eliminate craving for reclining and lying down;
one remains on a seat as usual in order to eliminate craving for bedding.
This is called accomplishing the dhūta qualities.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One should know that herein, if based on the undifferentiated nature of alms-gathering, there are only twelve;
if based on the differentiated nature of alms-gathering, there are thirteen."
Regarding those who practice seated meditation during both winter and summer:
in winter it is extremely cold,
and in summer it is extremely hot.
Furthermore, because injury and harm greatly obstruct wandering, sitting in stillness (*śamatha*) was prescribed.
As for those who enter the summer retreat (*varṣā*), they fix their minds on a single location and rely upon quiet conditions; therefore, it is called "dwelling in peace" (*an-ku*).
Unless there is an urgent necessity, one must not wander about recklessly.
However, if there is a place where benefit may be brought to oneself or others,
one may, according to circumstances, be granted permission to leave the boundary at sunrise.
Regarding the method of receiving the day [of ordination], one should apply it as appropriate according to the five divisions [of the Vinaya].
As for the common use of tooth-sticks and cleansing powder (*snāna-kṣāra*),
tooth-sticks are used regularly because they possess five virtues.
Soap powder is also used regularly for the sake of purification.
As for the eighteen items:
the three robes constitute three [items].
Fourth, the water flask;
fifth, the alms bowl;
sixth, the sitting mat.
7. The seven-fold mendicant’s staff;
8. The incense burner;
9. The water-strainer.
10. Hand-towels; 11. Knives; 12. Fire-sticks.
13. Tweezers. 14. A rope bed. 15. Scriptures.
16. Vinaya texts;
17. Buddha images; 18. Bodhisattva figures.
The first fourteen items are requisites for sustaining the body,
while the latter four are the supreme tracks for transcending the world;
therefore, they are prescribed so that one must always carry them and may not be separated from them.
The dhūta practitioner follows the seasonal regulations established from the first month of the year.
This is not merely for the sake of maintaining physical harmony during practice;
it also serves to establish a superior standard of conduct.
This should be understood as explained in the *Cittarāja-sūtra*.
If the Uposatha day arrives, the procedure for the Uposatha is to be performed according to the method set forth at the beginning of the sūtra.
The old commentary states:
"Because the minds of śrāvakas are weak,
they must rely on four or more people before they can recite it extensively."
The conduct of the Mahāsattvas is superior;
it is granted that even a single person may explain it extensively.
Now, it is said that even the extensive recitation by Śrāvakas is permitted.
However, one must not perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman).
Such is the principle within the Bodhisattva-dharma:
even if one has recited extensively, one must not perform the formal motion.
The reciter sits on a high seat while the listeners sit on lower seats;
this is for the sake of showing reverence for the Dharma.
The Vinaya also does not permit one sitting below to preach to those above.
Regarding the statement that each person wears a nine-striped, seven-striped, or five-striped *kāṣāya*,
one interpretation says:
"This text serves as proof for this."
The three robes may all be used for communal purposes.
One opinion states:
"This refers to wearing them together with the cloak."
As stated in the *Three Thousand Dignified Manners*:
"If one does not wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, one must not don the five-strip robe;

One who does not wear the seven-strip robe must not wear the nine-strip robe;

Regarding those who observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in every detail according to the Dharma:
When performing the formal acts of binding [the saṃgha], relying on a location, receiving [the precepts], emerging from the boundary, the invitation (pravāraṇā),

the formal censure (utkṣepana), or the confession (pratideśanā), all should be carried out in accordance with the Vinaya. When practicing the dhūta ascetic practices, do not enter difficult places or descend [to lower levels].
This section distinguishes the practice of *dhūta* austerities and the selection of locations for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) to avoid dangers.
Regarding the regulations established herein from beginning to end,
one tradition states:
The principles for monastics and laypeople are entirely the same. One source states:
"In traveling, staying, teaching, or transforming others, one must not recklessly expose oneself to danger."
This rule applies universally to both monastics and laypeople; however,
regarding the rules for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) and the confession ceremony (*poṣadha*), which require one to remain seated,
these apply only to the five classes of ordained monastics.
The *Upāsaka-sūtra* states:
"An upāsaka should possess the saṃghāṭī robe, the alms bowl, and the mendicant’s staff.

There is no offense. **The Eighth Precept on the Order of Seniority** If a Buddha’s disciple should sit according to the proper order of dharma: those who received the precepts first shall sit in front; those who received the precepts later shall sit behind. Whether they are old or young, whether they are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, nobles, kings, princes, or even eunuchs and slaves, all should sit such that those who received the precepts first are in front, and those who received the precepts later sit in succession behind them. Do not act like the foolish people of external paths, who—whether old or young—sit without priority or sequence, following the manner of soldiers or slaves. In my Buddha-dharma, the earlier receives precedence and the later sits behind. If a Bodhisattva does not sit according to this order, they commit a light secondary offense (*āpatti*). This is prescribed in order to abandon arrogance and to accord with the teachings of the Dharma.
Both the great and the small are equally restrained;
monastics and laypeople alike shall study this together.
Within the Vinaya, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"Who do you think should receive the first seat, the first water, and the first food, as well as rising to welcome and see them off, prostrating, showing respect, and exchanging polite greetings?
Some replied, "One who is born of a great clan."
Some say it is one whose countenance is upright and handsome;
some say it is an araṇya-dweller;
and some say it is a beggar for alms.
Some spoke of those who wear rag-robes;
and so on, until some spoke of those who are able to chant,
or those who are of great learning.
Some called him a Dharma Master;
some called him an Upadhāyaka (one who upholds the Vinaya);
and some called him a practitioner of seated meditation.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I shall now cite the past causes and conditions regarding the mutual respect shown by the elephant, the wildcat, and the quail.
You who have gone forth within my Dharma and Vinaya should likewise show mutual respect toward one another."
In this way, the Buddha-dharma may be propagated.
From this day forward, it is permitted for you to pay respectful homage according to seniority, welcoming and seeing off those of higher rank, and inquiring after their well-being.
Furthermore, it was said:
One should not pay homage to laypeople.
One should not pay homage to any women. Nor should one pay homage to those who received the full precepts (mahāśramaṇa) prior to oneself.
Regarding those who receive the full ordination (upasampadā) later:

one should not pay homage to those who possess the thirteen grounds for defeat (pārājika), those who have been formally censured three times (tri-utkṣepaṇīya-karman), those who have committed the two types of extinction (nihsargika-pācattika), or anyone who speaks in an entirely unlawful manner.
What kind of person should be paid homage?
A junior śrāmaṇerikā should pay homage to a senior śrāmaṇerikā;
likewise, she should pay homage to all such persons as śrāmaṇeras, śikṣamāṇās, bhikṣuṇīs, and bhikṣus, as well as their stūpas.
A young śrāmaṇera should pay homage to an elder śrāmaṇerī;
likewise, he should pay homage to all, from śikṣamāṇās down to bhikṣus and stūpas.
A junior śikṣamāṇā should pay homage to an elder śikṣamāṇā.
A bhikṣuṇī should pay homage to a bhikṣu and to a stūpa.
A junior bhikṣuṇī should pay homage to a senior bhikṣuṇī;
she should also pay homage to a bhikṣu and to a stūpa.
A junior bhikṣu should pay homage to a senior bhikṣu;
he should also pay homage to the stūpa of a senior bhikṣu.
This is because within the Dharma of Śākyamuni, it is stated that there is no separate community of bodhisattvas.
This accords with the disciplinary practices mentioned above and is consistent with principle.
Regarding the phrase "those who sit according to the sequence of the Dharma," it means as follows:
This means that the sequence of ascending and descending does not contradict the Buddha’s regulations;
however, regarding the ritual procedures for this practice, various masters differ in their views.
One school asserts as follows:
In all cases, receiving the bodhisattva precepts is the sequential priority.

A bhikṣu who has been ordained for a hundred years may receive the bodhisattva precepts after a bhikṣu who has been ordained for only one year, provided that the latter received the bodhisattva precepts first.
Thus, a bhikṣu of one year’s standing would sit in the front seat,
while a bhikṣu of a hundred years’ standing would sit in the rear seat;
for among men and women, the noble and the lowly, and all distinct classes, even if they had received the precepts earlier, [the seniority remained as described].
They must not be intermingled.
If a slave first receives [the title] from his master and later receives it from another,
then the slave is placed above and the master below.
This is because those who have already entered the dharma of the precepts do not follow their original status;
thus, it is stated twice.
If one has not yet received the bodhisattva precepts, [the procedure is as follows].
All [the senior monks] shall remain below those who have previously received the Bodhisattva precepts.
If they subsequently receive the precepts, they shall return to their original positions.
This is like a bhikṣu of a hundred years' standing who has not yet received [the Bodhisattva precepts], while a bhikṣu of one year's standing has already received them.
Those who have already received [the precepts] are superior;
those who have not yet received them are inferior.
Even one who is a hundred years old, if they advance to receive them, returns to the superior position.
The same applies to the master and the slave.
If the slave has already received [the precepts] while the master has not yet received them,
then the slave is superior and the master is inferior.
If a *rājan* (junior official) advances to receive [ordination], he still remains above a slave;
since both are equally bound by the precepts, they should follow their original status.
For example, if a *śrāmaṇera* advances to receive [ordination], he then stands above a nun of a hundred years' seniority.
Recite this three times.
Regarding dignified deportment and seating order, follow the sequence of the Śrāvaka Dharma;
do not inquire about the distinctions between Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
However, the one who received ordination first is considered superior.
If a śrāvaka bhikṣu has ten years of seniority and a bodhisattva bhikṣu has nine years,
the one with ten years is still considered superior.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The Buddhas mostly take śrāvakas as their saṃgha;
there is no separate bodhisattva saṃgha."
Just as Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, and others,
because there was no separate bodhisattva saṃgha for Śākyamuni Buddha,
entered among the śrāvaka saṃgha and sat in their respective order.
This text merely states that those who received [the precepts] earlier sit in front,
while those who received them later sit behind;
it does not distinguish between the śrāvaka and bodhisattva precepts.
Since there is no fixed age for a lay bodhisattva,
they all take the bodhisattva precepts as their standard of seniority;
it is therefore said that even within the household, one should likewise prioritize the reception of the precepts.
Whether one receives the five precepts of a śrāvaka or the five precepts of a bodhisattva,
that which was received first is superior.
If a slave first receives [an offering] and later a master receives it,
one may not treat the slave's reception as the subsequent order;
for the status of slave and master are distinct.
Because they are fundamentally not intermingled;
even if a slave were released and made a gentleman,
he should follow and receive his place in the sequence accordingly.
In worldly affairs, one generally follows the latter explanation.
Regarding "without regard to old or young," this does not refer to the age of one's years since birth.
In the Vinaya, the order of precedence for śrāmaṇeras is determined by their year of birth;
where years of birth are equal, the order is determined by the sequence of their ordination.
Since this text states that one does not inquire whether they are old or young, [the principle of seniority based on age is not applied here].
This is because it does not follow the order of their years of birth;
"bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs" refers to the two assemblies each receiving ordination according to their own sequence.
It does not mean that those who received the bhikṣuṇī ordination first are placed after those who received the bhikṣu ordination later.
Because the distinctions between male and female, as well as noble and humble, are fundamentally not intermingled,
the social hierarchy of the secular world is distinguished as previously explained.
Regarding the absence of a fixed order of seating, this follows the custom for soldiers and slaves.
In the military, those who are strong are prioritized,
regardless of seniority or age; however,
the Dharma and the Way are honored and should not be treated in such a manner.

Chapter Nine: The Precept of Gathering People through Merit and Wisdom. If a Buddha’s disciple, they should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings, establishing monasteries, mountain forests, gardens, and fields.
One should establish Buddha-stūpas and places for winter and summer retreats and seated meditation;
these should be established at all locations where one practices the Path.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings,
except on occasions such as times of illness, national calamities, or threats from bandits, or on the days when one's parents, brothers, preceptors (upādhyāya), or teachers (ācārya) have passed away.
Furthermore, during the third week, the fourth or fifth week, and even up to the seventh week,
one should likewise recite, chant, and expound upon the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya.

At all assemblies for purification (*poṣadha*) seeking merit, whether traveling for livelihood, or when afflicted by great fires, swept away by great floods, blown by black winds, or facing the perils of ships, rivers, oceans, and *rākṣasa* demons— [in all such cases, one should do so].
Furthermore, one should read, recite, and expound this sutra and vinaya.

Even for those who have committed all manner of karmic offenses resulting in the three evil realms, the seven heinous crimes, or the eight difficulties; those whose bodies are bound by cangues, manacles, and shackles; and those with excessive lust, anger, ignorance, or illness—all such individuals should read, recite, and expound this sutra and vinaya.
If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not act accordingly, they commit a minor offense (light defilement). Both merit and wisdom are like the two wheels or two wings of a vehicle;
if either one is lacking, it is difficult to attain the supreme fruit.
Therefore, it was established that the training in the common and uncommon precepts of both the Great and Small Vehicles should be practiced by all seven classes of disciples.
Within this passage, there are two parts.
First, to teach and transform others so that they may cultivate the karma of merit;
second, to lecture and explain the Dharma so that they may cultivate the karma of wisdom.
Regarding the first, one should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings, and even at every place where the Path is practiced, one should establish [the Dharma] there.
This means that although there are many gateways for cultivating meritorious deeds,
regarding their essentials,
I shall first explain the establishment of places for practicing the Way.
One should transform others according to one's strength and capacity;
even if one lacks the power to do so oneself,
one must not fail to exhort others to cultivate and give rise to wisdom.
Regarding the statement that one should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings:
this refers to those who possess understanding and wisdom,
meaning they have the capacity to expound them for others.
If one falls ill, there is a specific section clarifying that there are occasions where it is difficult to repay one's gratitude;
this shall also be expounded.
For now, ten such instances are enumerated.
First is the difficulty of illness,
which refers to times when the land is plagued by many diseases.
Second is the difficulty of the state.
This refers to the three calamities of bandits that occur when an evil king governs the world,
specifically during times when wicked people commit acts of invasion and violence.
Fourth, at the time when those who are honored pass away;
fifth, at the time of coming and going for the sake of livelihood.
According to some versions of the sūtra, it says "at the end of the practice, when one is about to be born."
Sixth, the calamities of water, fire, and wind;
seventh, the calamity of rākṣasas;
eighth, all retributions for transgressions.
That is to say: the three types of retribution, the eight difficulties, and even the binding of the body;
ninth, an abundance of afflictions;
tenth, an abundance of diseases.
This refers to having illness within one's own body.
Generally, there are ten matters for which one should preach the Sūtras and Vinaya,
so that others may be freed from various calamities and transform their karmic obstacles.
By refining and polishing [the mind], divine wisdom increases;
if one does not do so, it is contrary to the rule and constitutes an offense.

These nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart, as will be explained in the "Chapter on the Brahma-Altar. The phrase "these nine" and below serves as a concluding summary that points to the remainder.
2. The Second Section on the Nine Precepts:
Among these nine precepts, the first five are embraced by the dharma of the precepts, while the latter four are taught through the mind of compassion.
Of the preceding [five], the first three clarify the bestowing of the dharma of the precepts upon others;
the latter two clarify the internal upholding of the dharma of the precepts by the bodhisattva himself,
because he upholds them for himself and causes others to follow and learn from him.
Although this is for one's own benefit, it is in fact for the benefit of others.
Among the first three [points],
the first clarifies that for those who possess the capacity as vessels, one bestows [the teaching] without discriminating regarding the circumstances.
The second clarifies instructing those with obstacles to repent and eliminate them;
the third clarifies not rashly explaining [the teachings] to those who have not yet received them. 1.

Not Discerning Whether One is Capable of Receiving the Precepts. First, regarding not discerning whether one is capable of receiving the precepts, the Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, when bestowing the precepts upon others..."

There shall be no discrimination. All kings, princes, ministers, and officials; bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; male and female lay followers; men and women of loose conduct; the eighteen Brahmās and the six classes of gods of the desire realm; those without sexual organs, those with dual organs, and eunuchs; slaves; and all ghosts and spirits—every one of these may receive the precepts.
One should instruct that all the saṃghāṭī robes worn on the body be dyed in discolored hues to accord with the Way,
staining them blue, yellow, red, black, or purple.
All dyed robes, including even bedding and requisites, shall be entirely of a discolored hue.
All clothing worn on the body shall be dyed.
In all lands, whatever garments people of the country wear, the bhikṣus must ensure their secular dress differs from it.
When one wishes to receive the precepts, the master should ask:
"In this present life, have you not committed any of the seven heinous offenses?
A Bodhisattva Dharma Master must not confer the precepts upon a person who has committed one of the seven heinous offenses in their current existence.
The seven heinous offenses are:

shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing one’s preceptor (upādhyāya), killing one’s ācārya, disrupting the Saṃgha that is performing the *karmavācanā* for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and killing an arhat.
If one possesses the seven obstructions, one cannot receive the precepts in this present life;
all other persons may fully receive the precepts.
According to the dharma for those who have left the household life, one does not prostrate before kings.
They do not prostrate to their parents;
they show no reverence to their six kin, nor do they offer worship to the spirits and deities.
They understand only the words of the Dharma Master.
If there are those who come from a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Dharma,
yet the Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, does not immediately bestow the precepts for all sentient beings upon them.
Regarding the transgression of a minor offense: if there are those with the capacity who are fit to receive [the precepts], one should bestow them upon all such persons.
If one discriminates against them out of anger or resentment, it violates the principle of providing guidance.
Therefore, the regulations are not restrictive.
Bodhisattvas who seek to receive [the precepts] must not fail to do so,
because they have made original vows to provide universal salvation.
If one consents to a proposal and later regrets it, it is an offense;
if one did not consent from the outset, there is no offense.
This applies equally to all seven classes of practitioners.

Since the Sūtra permits husbands and wives to act as preceptors for one another, the text states that when conferring the precepts upon others, one must not exercise discrimination; even those [normally excluded] are permitted to receive the precepts.
Thus, seventeen categories of persons are cited, all of whom are allowed to receive the precepts.
In this passage, there is no distinction made between laypeople and monastics, nor between novices (śrāmaṇera) and fully ordained monks;
it simply states that they "may receive" [the precepts].
If one follows the subsequent text:
The teaching requires one to change from local customs and to be permitted to leave the household life.
However, there are two ways of receiving the Dharma.
If one follows the Vinaya rules for receiving the precepts individually,

one must carefully examine whether the candidate is free from disqualifications such as being rootless (*amūlaka*). If, however, one relies on the general reception of the Three Refuges and the Three Aggregates (*triskandhaka*), [such examination is not required].
Since the scriptural passage is not restrictive,

it should logically be understood as permitting [the reception of all five precepts]. This is analogous to the case of *paṇḍaka*s and others, who are permitted to receive the five precepts while being barred from the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
In this context, one must also admit that although full ordination (*upasampadā*) is granted, the status of being a bhikṣu and so forth is excluded;
for while the text contains no specific distinction, the meaning determines it.
Those who possess wisdom should further seek the teachings; specifically,
one should instruct that the *kāṣāya* worn on the body below [the waist] clearly demonstrates the rejection of worldly finery in accordance with the robes of the Way.
Regarding the term "altering the color":
it means altering that primary color to produce an irregular color.
"Being in accord with the Path" means:
Because they destroy worldly preferences, they should wear the robes of the Way.
As for dyeing them blue, yellow, red, black, or purple:
because the five schools of the Hīnayāna hold differing views, each school wears robes of a single color.
Because the Bodhisattva has no partial attachment to the five [colors], he wears robes of all five colors.
These five mentioned, such as blue and so forth,
all refer to those that have been dyed into blue and the other colors.
"It is not that the great colors such as blue and so forth [are forbidden];
rather, even bedding must all be dyed with a discolored hue.
This means that it is not only the three robes that must be dyed with a discolored hue.
All clothing, even down to bedding, shall likewise be dyed with the three types of discoloration (*kāṣāya*).
As for the garments worn on the body, even those that are inferior to the local dress of the land,
their color must differ [from that of the laity].
This is to cause one's appearance to differ from that of the laity. As for those things that differ from the clothing of the laity,
the methods for making them are likewise intended to differ from the laity.
Since it has already been stated that [this applies to] bhikṣus,
one should not generalize this to the laity.
As for the old teaching that both monastics and laypeople must wear dyed (ruined-color) robes:
No. It is as stated below regarding the time of receiving the precepts:
one eliminates heavy obstacles to become a pure vessel.
The seven heinous offenses are grave obstructions.
If one commits them in this present life, one cannot become a vessel for receiving the precepts.
If one were to undergo the ritual procedure for ordination without such discernment, one would ultimately achieve nothing;
therefore, it is necessary to distinguish them. From among the thirteen *ānantarya* (grave offenses), one must specifically select the five *ānantarya* (parricides, matricides, etc.).
Furthermore, harming one's teacher constitutes the seventh immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
As for the names of these seven,
the first is shedding the blood of a Buddha.
Second, killing one's father;
third, killing one's mother;
fourth, killing one's preceptor.
Fifth, killing an ācārya;
sixth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha that obstructs the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
seventh, killing an arhat.
Regarding those who break the *karmavācanā*, the wheel of Dharma,
and the Saṃgha: one interpretation holds that only the breaking of the wheel of Dharma constitutes an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).

If one causes a schism in the Saṃgha regarding formal procedures (karmavācanā), it is not an immediate transgression (ānantarya). This is because at the time of causing a schism in the Saṃgha regarding formal procedures,
one does not intend to engage in dispute, but rather gives rise to a different view.
However, when the Wheel of Dharma is destroyed, because the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts) are ruined,
it is called "the Sangha that destroys the *karmavācanā* and turns back the Wheel of Dharma."
One interpretation of this treatise states:
Destroying the Wheel of Dharma is invariably a heinous crime (ānantarya),
whereas destroying the ritual procedure (karmavācanā) should be analyzed with distinctions.
If one breaks [the Saṃgha] with the perception that it is a Dharma, this is not a pāyattika offense.
If one breaks it with the perception that it is not the Dharma,
for a śrāvaka, this is not a pāyattika offense.
For a bodhisattva, this constitutes a heinous offense (ānantarya),
just as it does for one who harms two teachers or a noble being on the path of training (śaikṣa);
however, for a śrāvaka, it is not a heinous offense.
For a bodhisattva, this would be a transgression;
this case should likewise be understood in the same way.
As for one who kills a noble person (ārya):
This includes both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This differs from the case among the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), where only the harming of one beyond training is included.
When comparing bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, one should distinguish between what constitutes a grave offense and what does not by means of four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
First, those that are difficult for śrāvakas but not for bodhisattvas refer to the eight [obstacles] among the thirteen, excluding the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
Second, those that are difficult for bodhisattvas but not for śrāvakas...
That is to say, among the seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*), killing a trainee (*śaikṣa*) or an *arhat*, and causing a schism in the *karmavācanā* Sangha,

constitute such offenses; however, harming the two teachers (father and mother) does not constitute a heinous offense [in this specific context], because they are categorized among the eight secondary offenses (*pārājika*).
Even among those śrāvakas, it is difficult to gather them;
for one who kills a noble person in training,
there is the obstacle of the eighth pārājika offense for one who has previously received the precepts.
That which has never been experienced before is not difficult.
Third, that which is difficult for both [the practitioner and the listener] refers to the five heinous crimes (ānantarya).
Regarding those who are exempt from these difficulties:
this excludes the aforementioned cases.
If one possesses the seven types of prohibitions (*saptāvaraṇa*), one shall not obtain the precepts in this very life.
Thus, because the seven aforementioned transgressions can obstruct the precepts, they are termed "obstructive" (*āvaraṇa*).
This term possesses two meanings:
first, because they constitute a full karmic action when all conditions are met, they are termed "complete" (*samanvāgata*).
This excludes those cases of immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) where the necessary conditions are incomplete.
Second, within a single lifetime, all seven immediate transgressions may be committed;
that is to say, for one who has previously received full ordination as a great bhikṣu, it is possible to commit all seven within that same lifetime.
If one has never committed the two offenses of harming a teacher or causing a schism in the Sangha, nor any of the other immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*),
then according to the latter interpretation,
one should be able to receive [the precepts] even if not all seven immediate transgressions are present.
Answer: No. This is stated by way of the maximum possible case, wherein one who possesses all seven prohibitions (*saptāvaraṇa*) cannot presently receive the precepts;
it does not mean that committing each individual *ānantarya* (heinous offense) fails to constitute a prohibitory obstruction.
If it were not so, there would be no need to ask further after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
for it would be said that there is no such thing as causing a schism in the Saṃgha or shedding the blood of a Buddha.
The dharma of those who have left the household life is that they do not prostrate to kings, nor even to ghosts and spirits;
this demonstrates that the Way is honored.
By saying "those who have left the household life," he distinguishes them from those who remain at home.
A lay bodhisattva, having already conformed to worldly etiquette,
commits no transgression even when prostrating before those who are revered.
As for spirits and deities:
If one prostrates to worldly spirits for the sake of seeking merit,
it is not permitted even for a layperson who has received the precepts; however,
this does not apply if one knows with certainty that the being is a spirit manifesting through skillful means (*upāya*).
There is no offense for a lay bodhisattva to perform this prostration;
however, if one understands the teacher’s words and then acts contrary to them, it constitutes an offense. 2.
The Second Precept on Being a Virtuous Teacher: O disciples of the Buddha, when you teach and transform others so that they give rise to faith, [you must act as follows].
When a bodhisattva acts as a teacher and instructor for others,
upon seeing a person who wishes to receive the precepts,
they should instruct them to request two masters: an upādhyāya and an ācārya.
The two masters should ask:
"Do you have any of the seven obstructing offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*)?
If, in this present life, one has committed any of the seven obstructing offenses, [one is ineligible].
The preceptor should not confer the precepts upon them.

Because of such slander, just as one who abides in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline achieves an immeasurable treasury of great merit,

**The Fifth Precept on Making Offerings to the Scriptures:** If a Buddha’s disciple constantly and with single-minded devotion upholds, recites, and studies the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, they should—even if it means flaying their skin for paper, piercing their blood for ink, using marrow as water, and breaking their bones for pens—transcribe the Buddha’s precepts. Whether using tree bark, mulberry paper, silk, or bamboo slips, they must likewise transcribe and maintain them. They should always use the seven treasures, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels to fashion cases and bags to hold the volumes of the sūtras and vinaya. If one does not make such offerings in accordance with the Dharma, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). The Dharma is the mold that opens the way for the spirit.
One must especially show them respect;
if one fails to protect them according to the Dharma,
there will be much deficiency in one's practice.
Therefore, it is established that they must maintain reverence;
those within the seven assemblies who study together do not share the same status, whether senior or junior.

Furthermore, one should first allow one's parents, teachers, and elders to enjoy it,
